title: Photosynthesis & Light
objectives: Measure the rate of photosynthesis by counting oxygen bubbles
Use the inverse square law to explain how light intensity changes with distance
Identify a limiting factor and connect photosynthesis to the carbon cycle (APES 1.5, 9.4)

npcLines: Every bubble rising from this Elodea plant is oxygen made by photosynthesis. More bubbles per minute means faster photosynthesis.
Use the bench on the right. Keep the bicarbonate at 1% and the water at 25 °C, and change only the lamp distance. That's a fair test.

sequence.instruction: Run a 1-minute trial with the lamp at 10 cm (1% bicarbonate, 25 °C).
Run a trial with the lamp at 20 cm.
Run a trial with the lamp at 30 cm.
Run a trial with the lamp at 40 cm.

feedback.correct: 40 cm trial recorded. You now have a data set.

question.prompt: How many bubbles per minute did you count with the lamp at 20 cm?

feedback.incorrect: Check the 20 cm row of your trials table.

question.prompt: Light intensity follows the inverse square law. At 20 cm, what fraction of the 10 cm light intensity reaches the plant? (Give a decimal.)

sequence.hint: Doubling the distance gives (1/2)² of the light.

sequence.instruction: Now run a trial at 10 cm with 0% bicarbonate (no added CO₂).

feedback.correct: Trial recorded. Compare it with your 10 cm, 1% trial.

question.prompt: With the lamp at 10 cm but no added bicarbonate, the rate dropped sharply. What was limiting photosynthesis?

feedback.correct: Right: plenty of light, but not enough CO₂ to build sugar.
feedback.incorrect: Light was at its strongest. What did you remove?

question.prompt: Ocean phytoplankton and forests do the same photosynthesis as Elodea. Explain how they act as carbon sinks, and describe one human activity that weakens them.
